what: One row per Act we hold.
why: Everything about a law hangs off its Act: its versions and its sections.
madeBy: pipeline/load_acts.py, from the Archive copies of Kenya Law's pages
columns: Its Cap. number in the Laws of Kenya
Kenya Law's own address for the Act

what: One row per dated version of an Act.
why: Acts change over time. Keeping every version lets us show that s.204's words never changed after Muruatetu.

what: One row per section, the same across versions.
why: Events attach to a section, not to one version's text, so a ruling in 2017 still applies to the 2023 version.

what: A section's words in one version, plus search data.
why: Search runs over these: by exact words (tsv) and by meaning (embedding).
columns: Any person convicted of murder shall be sentenced to death.

what: One row per court judgment: details only, the full text stays on disk.
why: The filing checker needs to know whether a cited case exists. Events need to say which judgment did what.
columns: Our ID: jurisdiction + court + year + number
Where the full text is on disk

what: Every place a judgment cites a section: step 5's output.
why: It narrows 16,419 judgments down to the ones worth reading for events, and tells us where in each judgment to look.
madeBy: pipeline/extract_citations.py (patterns), then pipeline/llm_resolve.py (LLM, for bare mentions)
columns: Which section, if it's one of our 8 Acts
Which law it cites, even if we don't hold it
Found by a pattern or by the LLM
How sure we are which law it is

what: What a court (or Parliament) actually did to a section. This table is the project.
why: Status is worked out from these events. Each one carries the court's exact words, so every answer can show its source. Machine-found rows stay unverified until a person checks them, and the API leaves them out unless asked.
madeBy: The answer key (method = manual), then pipeline/classify_events.py (method = extracted, unverified), checked by pipeline/verify_events.py
columns: The judgment that did it (empty for Acts of Parliament)
to the extent that it provides for the mandatory death sentence
The court's words making the order, exactly
The mandatory nature of the death sentence … is hereby declared unconstitutional.
The earlier event this one directly acts on (an appeal)
Who made it, and whether a person checked it
The second-pass checker's verdict on an extracted event (fail = hidden)

what: Which judgments the event classifier has already read.
why: It tells "read, and found nothing" apart from "not read yet". Without it, a missing event is ambiguous.

what: The answer key: 19 events on 11 sections, each checked by hand against the judgment.
why: It's both reliable demo data and the benchmark the automatic classifier is scored against. A check script confirms every quote appears word for word in the judgment.
madeBy: Drafted, audited blind by a second model, verified by a third, final call by Leo. ground_truth/check.py re-verifies it
columns: The row this one directly acts on

what: Six judgments that mention a focus section but do nothing to it.
why: The easiest mistake is "this judgment mentions s.204, so it changed s.204". These catch it. So far the classifier raises 0 of 6 false alarms.
columns: murder trial; s.204 only recited in the charge

what: Random samples of machine-found events, each judged by two reviewers who couldn't see each other's answers.
why: The answer key only covers 19 events the prompt was tuned on, so it flatters the classifier. Fresh random samples give the honest number: about 53% right at first, about 80% after the fixes and the second-pass checker.
madeBy: ground_truth/events_review_sample.py draws each sample; eval_events_review.py and eval_checker.py score them
columns: Is it a real event on the right section?
follows Muruatetu; no holding of its own

what: Hand-labelled citations from 30 random judgments, and a second 30 kept aside (the held-out set).
why: It measures step 5. The held-out set was never used to tune the patterns, so its score (98.1% precision and recall) is the honest one.
madeBy: Labelled, then checked by independent reviewers who never saw the extractor
columns: section 8(1) of the Sexual Offences Act
